title: Stanley's Lumber Mill Needed a Dam Before It Needed Buildings
summary: Before Stanley's huge lumber operation could take shape, a dam was built across the Wolf River to create the mill pond that later became Chapman Lake. Only then did the company build the industrial complex that would employ hundreds.

title: Hundreds Worked at Stanley's Huge Northwestern Lumber Company Mill
summary: The Northwestern Lumber Company built a major sawmill complex beside its Wolf River mill pond at Stanley. The operation employed hundreds and became one of the defining industries in the community before the mill closed in 1922.

title: Stanley's Mill Had a 'Hot Pond'
summary: Among the specialized features of Stanley's Northwestern Lumber Company complex was a hot pond used in the mill operation. The Stanley Area Historical Society preserves photographs and interpretation of the pond and the enormous mill system around it.

title: A Steam Engine Hauled 16 Loads of Logs Through the Woods Without Tracks
summary: Stanley's lumber operation used an extraordinary steam-powered hauling engine capable of pulling sixteen loads of logs through the woods without running on railroad tracks—a mechanized answer to moving enormous quantities of timber in winter.

title: Stanley's Lumber Company Built Its Own Railroad Into the Northwoods
summary: The Stanley, Merrillan & Phillips Railroad began in Stanley as part of the region's lumber economy. Its tracks eventually stretched north as far as Wallrath, carrying both logs and passengers through the forest country.

title: A Logging Railroad From Stanley Carried People as Well as Timber
summary: The Stanley, Merrillan & Phillips Railroad was more than an industrial logging line. Historical Society exhibits document that it also carried people while extending north from Stanley toward Wallrath.

title: Stanley's Lumber Workers Lived in Company Housing Called the Red Row Houses
summary: The Northwestern Lumber Company shaped daily life as well as employment in Stanley. Its industrial community included company housing remembered locally as the Red Row Houses.

title: Stanley's Lumber Empire Had Its Own Company Store
summary: Workers in Stanley's vast lumber operation lived within a company-centered industrial community that included a company store, housing and the sprawling mill complex around the Wolf River pond.

title: When Stanley's Lumber Mill Closed, the Company Gave Its 81-Acre Mill Pond to the City
summary: After the Northwestern Lumber Company closed its Stanley mill in 1922, it donated the 81-acre mill-pond property to the people of Stanley. The former industrial landscape became Chapman Lake Park.
location: Chapman Lake Park, Stanley, Chippewa County

title: Stanley's Chapman Lake Is Really an Old Lumber Mill Pond
summary: The lake at the center of Stanley's Chapman Park did not begin as a natural recreational lake. It originated when the Northwestern Lumber Company dammed the Wolf River to create a pond needed for its sawmill operation.

title: Chapman Lake Park Was Named for the Man Who Managed Stanley's Lumber Mill
summary: When Stanley's former lumber-company mill pond became public parkland, it was named Chapman Lake Park for George Chapman, the manager of the Northwestern Lumber Company mill.

title: The First Thorp Settler's Nearest Neighbor Was Ten Miles Away
summary: When James Seneca Boardman settled in the country that became Thorp and Withee in 1870, his nearest settler neighbor lived about ten miles away near Longwood. The nearest post office was at Greenwood.

title: A Thorp Pioneer Hauled Handmade Shingles 50 Miles by Ox Sled
summary: James Seneca Boardman made shaved shingles during winter, loaded them onto a sled and hauled them roughly fifty miles to Black River Falls. He sold them for supplies and made the long trip home with a yoke of cattle.

title: A Supply Trip From Early Thorp Took Nine Days by Ox Team
summary: Before railroads and developed roads reached the Thorp area, James Boardman's winter trip to Black River Falls to sell shingles and buy supplies took nine days by ox team.

title: Early Thorp Settlers Blazed Roads Through Forest With No Trail to Follow
summary: Some of Thorp's earliest settlers entered a landscape with no roads and, according to local historical accounts, not even an Indigenous trail along the routes they needed. They blazed rough roads near section lines and moved families and belongings into the forest.

title: A Diphtheria Outbreak Left Only One Student in a Thorp School District
summary: Diphtheria devastated pioneer families around Thorp in 1879. Historical accounts list eleven deaths among several families and report that, after the epidemic, Eddie Fults was the only student left in School District No. 1.

title: Two Thorp Families Each Lost Four Children to Diphtheria
summary: The 1879 diphtheria epidemic struck Thorp with extraordinary cruelty. Historical accounts say James Boardman and his wife lost four children, while C. C. Clark and his wife also lost four children during the outbreak.

title: Thorp's Railroad Bond Was Voided Because Signatures Were Collected on Sunday
summary: Thorp approved a bond connected with railroad construction, but the bond was declared invalid because many of its signatures had been obtained on a Sunday. Railroad construction nevertheless moved ahead in 1880.

title: Thorp Was First a Railroad Station Spelled 'Thorpe'
summary: When railroad track reached the community in November 1880, the railroad company named its station 'Thorpe.' That winter the local post office changed its name from North Fork to Thorp, dropping the final 'e.'

title: Before It Was Thorp, the Community Was Called North Fork
summary: The settlement that became Thorp was originally known as North Fork. Its post office officially adopted the name Thorp after the railroad arrived in 1880.

title: Thorp's Town Clerk Forged Public Orders and Fled
summary: In 1882 Thorp town clerk Charles Sheldon forged town orders worth about $250 and fled. He was later captured, convicted and sentenced to eighteen months of hard labor at Waupun.

title: Thorp's First Newspaper Lasted Only Twelve Weeks
summary: Thorp's first newspaper, The Pioneer, began publication in May 1883 but suspended operations after only twelve weeks. New owners acquired its equipment, added improved type and launched the Thorp Courier later that year.

title: Thorp Voters Rejected Becoming a Village 79 to 38
summary: Thorp's first serious attempt to incorporate as a village failed in 1886. A special election at Sargent's Hall produced 79 votes against incorporation and only 38 in favor.

title: A Thorp Dairy Shipped More Than 1.8 Million Pounds of Cheese in One Year
summary: By 1916 the Thorp Dairy Company had become a major rural processor. Historical records report that it shipped 1,832,788 pounds of cheese and 279,785 pounds of butter during that year.

title: Thorp Dairy Once Controlled Six Creameries
summary: The Thorp Dairy Company expanded beyond its home creamery beside the railroad. By 1917 it owned the village creamery plus five additional plants in surrounding communities.

title: Thorp's Library Began With Just 120 Books in a Newspaper Office
summary: Before Thorp had a dedicated library building, its public library operated from the Thorp Courier printing office with only 120 volumes. A local women's club bought many of its books and even helped convert a woodshed into a reading room.

title: A Women's Club Paid to Turn Thorp's Woodshed Into a Reading Room
summary: Thorp's Women's Union Club supported the fledgling public library by purchasing books, paying for extra library hours and financing the conversion of a back room used as a woodshed into a reading room with a table and chairs.

title: The Settlement of Hemlock Once Controlled the Head of Clark County's Log Drives
locationAccuracy: historic Hemlock settlement, Town of Warner
summary: The vanished settlement of Hemlock grew around a dam on the Black River that marked the upper end of major log drives. Logs accumulated in the pond until water conditions were right, then the dam was opened to send water and timber downstream.
location: Hemlock, Town of Warner, Clark County

title: A Lost Clark County Hamlet Once Had a Sawmill, Flour Mill, Store and Eight Houses
summary: Hemlock was once a busy little industrial settlement. Historical accounts describe a sawmill, grist mill, boarding house, store and eight houses clustered around the Black River dam before the hamlet faded away.

title: Clark County's First Telephone Line Once Ended at a Now-Vanished Hamlet
summary: The old settlement of Hemlock was important enough that Clark County's first telephone line reportedly terminated there. Today the industrial hamlet itself has largely vanished from the landscape.

title: A 1914 Flood Destroyed Hemlock's Dam and Mills
summary: A major 1914 flood ended the old industrial era at Hemlock. Floodwaters tore out the dam and left hardly a trace of the sawmill and grist mill that had once supported the settlement.

title: A Clark County Mill Worker Thought His Shaking Sawmill Might Collapse
summary: As Hemlock's old sawmill deteriorated, workers could feel the building shake when heavy logs passed through the saw. A later historical account recalled that workers wondered whether the aging structure might shake itself apart.

title: A Clark County Lumber Heir Lived in an 18-Room House With Servants
summary: Theodore Withee lived at the family's Hemlock property in an expanded eighteen-room house. Historical recollections describe servants, comfortable living and a household very different from the rough logging camps surrounding it.

title: One of Clark County's First Fords Was Famous for Its Noise
summary: Theodore Withee owned one of Clark County's early Ford automobiles. Neighbors later recalled that they could tell when he was coming simply from the sound of the car approaching.

title: A Pioneer Clark County Settlement Once Rivaled Places That Later Became Cities
summary: Longwood appears prominently on early Clark County maps from a time when later communities such as Owen, Thorp and Withee were absent or insignificant. It served as an early post office and trading station before newer railroad towns eclipsed it.

title: Hemlock's Dam Cost $21,000 in 1879
summary: The Black River dam that helped make Hemlock an important lumbering and milling settlement was built in 1879 at a reported cost of $21,000—a major investment in Clark County's nineteenth-century timber economy.

title: Early Thorp Women Sang to Scare Wolves Away
summary: A local history of Thorp recalls that before the railroad opened the forest and brought more neighbors, settlers' wives left alone during winter would sing to frighten wolves away from their homes.

title: Thorp's First Fourth of July Also Hosted Its First Recorded Marriage
summary: The settlement then known as North Fork held its first Fourth of July celebration in 1876. Local history records that the same day also brought the area's first marriage, between Louis Bruno and Nora Warner.

title: Thorp's First Town Election Drew Only 29 Votes
summary: When the Town of Thorp was organized in 1876, only 29 votes were cast at its first town meeting. Residents nevertheless levied money for roads, bridges and schools as the isolated settlement began building local government.

title: Thorp's First Frame School Cost $1,600
summary: The newly organized Town of Thorp created two school districts in 1876. School District No. 1 soon erected a frame schoolhouse at a reported cost of $1,600.

title: A $30,000 High School Rose in Tiny Thorp Before World War I
summary: As Thorp grew, its earlier school buildings became inadequate. A new high school was completed by 1912 at a reported cost of $30,000, a substantial civic investment for the small community.
